# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

The first half of this comment is valuable. It uses the microdata to check three of the working paper's weakest points: attrition, the manager-rated output index, and the scheduled-hours denominator. It also brings a genuinely new finding: the nine withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule began, which contradicts the working paper's account.

The second half overreaches. The corrected figure, +10.8% output per actual hour, is still a substantial gain. The step from there to "entirely an artifact" rests on a novelty argument the authors could have tested and didn't. It also depends on reading the Varden trial selectively.

## Arithmetic checks

**These are correct:**
- Table 2: 98.7/0.800 = +23.4%; 95.1/0.800 = +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- Hours: 40.3 → 34.6 is −14.1%; 40.4 → 34.8 is −13.9%.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 = 0.974, a fall of 2.6%.

**The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Section 3 attributes the gap between scheduled and actual hours to two sources:
- an extra 0.7 hours a day on the four working days, which is about 2.8 hours a week;
- 1.6 hours a week logged on the day off.

Starting from 32 scheduled hours, that gives about 36.4 hours a week, or about 36.6 if the baseline's slightly long days (40.3/5) are carried over. The reported figure is 34.6. If the components are right, actual hours fell only about 9–10%, and the corrected per-hour gain is smaller still. If the 34.6 total is right, the extra time on working days is about 0.25 hours a day, not 0.7. Either way, one of these figures needs correcting.

**The novelty extrapolation is off.** Energy fell 0.32 SD between months 3 and 6, about 0.107 SD a month. At that rate it would reach baseline 2.7 months after month 6, at about month 9, not "around month ten". The difference is small, but the extrapolation is also doubtful in principle (see section 3 below).

**Two counts are incomplete:**
- Six withdrawals cited workload or output and two cited scheduling, which accounts for 8 of 9. The ninth reason should be given.
- 19 of 23 managers rated above the records. On a sign test this is very unlikely by chance (p ≈ 0.003, two-sided). The comment could report that number.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own estimate

The abstract and Section 8 say per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty". But the corrected estimate is +10.8%: record-based output against actual hours. That is a positive gain after measurement correction. So the "entirely" claim depends on two arguments the comment doesn't actually demonstrate.

**Selection is argued, not quantified.** Attrition doesn't enter Table 2. The abstract says "correcting the first three [problems], the gain… falls to 10.8%". In fact Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is the first of the four problems and is not corrected.

A bounding exercise would show how much attrition could matter. For example, impute output for the nine withdrawn organisations under pessimistic assumptions, or compute Lee-type bounds. If 10.8% survives plausible worst cases, the selection argument can't carry the conclusion.

**Novelty is asserted, not shown.** This is the weakest step; see section 3 below.

**The claim is generalised to all schemes.** The conclusion covers "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general. The evidence comes from a single pilot.

A conclusion the evidence supports would be something like: *"After correction, the per-hour gain is roughly halved, to about 11% in the subset with usable data. Selection and the short time horizon mean even this may overstate the durable effect."*

## 2. The use of the Varden trial is selective

The comment calls the Varden counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature". It doesn't mention the result from the other stratum of the same trial. In Varden's case-processing offices, output per actual hour rose 12.5% at nine months (CI +6.9 to +18.4). That result came with:
- randomisation;
- output from administrative records;
- actual hours from timesheets;
- a registered analysis plan.

These are close to the standards the comment's own recommendations set out, short only of the 18-month follow-up. The estimate is also close to the comment's corrected 10.8%.

This bears on the novelty argument too. Varden staff didn't choose the change; they were randomised into it. Yet the gain was present at month nine, beyond the point where the comment's extrapolation puts energy back at baseline. That doesn't prove the gain is durable, but it cuts against "entirely novelty". The comment should engage with it.

Calling the counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature" is also too strong. It rests on 5 v 5 offices with a wide confidence interval. "The only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work" is accurate and sufficient.

## 3. The novelty argument could have been tested directly

The Halden pilot collected the output index monthly. With the microdata, the authors can check whether output, or record-based output where it exists, declines from month 1 to month 6. That trajectory is what a novelty effect predicts. Instead the comment uses self-reported energy as a proxy, and the proxy has several problems:
- **Energy isn't output.** A fall in reported energy needn't mean a fall in productivity.
- **Two time points don't establish a trend.** They can't distinguish a linear decline from a decline that levels off above baseline.
- **Month three isn't the start.** The 0.61 SD rise at month three may itself be a peak, or a temporary adjustment.

"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a fair point about durability. It doesn't license the opposite claim, that the gain is an artifact. That is also a positive claim, and it needs its own evidence.

## 4. Table 2 compares different samples

The four rows use four different sets of organisations: 61, 23, 27 and 17. The change from row to row therefore mixes the effect of each correction with differences between the samples. The Data Note acknowledges this, but the table invites reading it as a sequence of corrections.

The fix is straightforward: compute all four specifications on the same 17 organisations. Doing so would:
- isolate the effect of each correction;
- show whether those 17 organisations' manager-reported, scheduled-hours estimate is itself close to 23.4%.

The abstract and conclusion should also carry the Data Note's caveat that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

## 5. Record-based output isn't automatically the true figure

Table 1 treats the records-based index as correct and the manager index as biased. That's reasonable on balance; the 19-of-23 pattern is persuasive. But one of the record types listed is "billable hours delivered", and that is an input measure, not output. Where billable hours are the output measure, output will fall almost mechanically with hours, which biases the record-based index toward finding no per-hour gain. The comment should do two things:
- report how many of the 23 (and of the 17) used billable hours;
- show the comparison with those organisations excluded.

Tickets closed and cases completed are also sensitive to task mix and complexity over the period. Those measures are better than manager ratings, but they can still be wrong.

## 6. The meetings section mischaracterises the Varden analysis

**What Varden actually said.** The Varden authors explicitly stated that the analysis was unregistered, rested on seven offices, and "cannot establish a mechanism". They also registered a confirmatory test. The comment's warning that it "should not be cited as a mechanism" therefore repeats the original authors' own caveat while implying they made a stronger claim.

**The offices weren't a selected subgroup.** The seven offices are the entire treated case-processing stratum. The comment says they were "selected for analysis after the results were known" and calls the account "fitted to a subgroup". Both overstate what happened. It is fair to call the analysis exploratory and the correlation unreliable.

**The meetings hypothesis cuts against the comment's argument.** If part of the gain comes from cutting low-value meetings, that is a real, potentially durable efficiency gain, not novelty. It is also a mechanism the comment's conclusion leaves no room for. The comment should engage with this rather than dismiss it.

## 7. Smaller points

**The attrition timeline needs clarifying.** The working paper describes a two-month preparation phase. Seven organisations withdrew in "the first month" and "the second", and it isn't clear whether these are the first two months of the pilot or of preparation. If some organisations began the reduced schedule during preparation, both accounts could be partly right. Either way, this is a significant correction to the working paper, and the comment should state it precisely.

**CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue.** Sector output prices, or producer prices for services, would suit better. The direction of the conclusion, that revenue fell in real terms, probably holds.

**Revenue doesn't affect the main estimate.** The abstract lists revenue among the "four problems [that] account for most of the reported gain". Revenue doesn't enter the per-hour calculation, so it can't account for any of the gain. It should be presented as a separate criticism.

**Some figures need uncertainty.** The retail figure for three organisations (−11.2%) needs that caveat stated alongside it, and confidence intervals would help throughout.

## Overall

Sections 1 to 5 are a useful correction to the Halden working paper, and they confirm several concerns that could only be inferred from the working paper: attrition during the pilot, inflation in the manager index, the gap between actual and scheduled hours, and the real-terms fall in revenue.

The comment would be stronger if it:
1. fixed the hours decomposition;
2. put all corrections on a common sample;
3. bounded the attrition effect;
4. tested novelty using the monthly output data;
5. engaged with Varden's case-processing result;
6. concluded that the durable per-hour gain is uncertain and probably much smaller than 23%, rather than nonexistent.

As written, its own best estimate contradicts its headline.
